los.text: Describe the milestones of normal development in childhood and during puberty and compare these to common alterations observed in clinical practice
los.html:
AgeGross motorFine motorSpeech/languageSocial
6 wkHead lag reducingFollows to midlineStartles to soundSocial smile
6 moSits with support, rollsPalmar grasp, transfers hand to handBabblesLaughs, stranger anxiety starts ~8 mo
9 moSits unsupported, crawls, pulls to standInferior pincer"Mama/dada" non-specificWaves bye-bye, peek-a-boo
12 moCruises / walks (by 18 mo = limit)Neat pincer1–3 wordsPoints
18 moWalks well, squatsTower of 3, scribbles6–20 wordsSpoon, symbolic play
2 yrRuns, kicks ballTower of 6, line2-word phrases, ~50 wordsParallel play
3 yrTricycle, stairs alternate feetCopies circle, tower of 93–4 word sentencesShares, plays with others
4 yrHopsCopies cross/squareTells storiesCooperative play
Red flags
  • Not smiling by 8 weeks
  • Not sitting by 9 months
  • Not walking by 18 months
  • No words by 18 months
  • Loss of skills at any age
  • Asymmetry
  • Hand preference before 12 months (suggests hemiplegia).
Puberty(Tanner stages 1–5)
  • Girls 8–13 (thelarche first → pubarche → growth spurt → menarche ~2.5 years later)
  • Boys 9–14 (testicular enlargement ≥4 mL first → pubarche → growth spurt later).
AlterationsGlobal developmental delay (genetic, hypoxic, metabolic), cerebral palsy (motor), autism (social/communication), hearing loss (speech), precocious/delayed puberty, constitutional delay.

los.text: Explain possible indicators of child abuse, the actions that may be taken and the Doctor's role and responsibility in safeguarding children
los.html:
TypesPhysical, emotional, sexual, neglect (commonest category on UK plans).
Indicators of physical abuse
  • Injury inconsistent with history or development ("those who don't cruise rarely bruise"), delayed presentation, changing story
  • Bruises on TEN-4 areas (Torso, Ears, Neck; any bruise under 4 months)
  • Patterned bruises
  • Cigarette burns
  • Immersion scalds (glove/stocking, sharp line)
  • Torn frenulum
  • Posterior rib fractures, metaphyseal "corner" fractures
  • Subdural haemorrhage/retinal haemorrhages (abusive head trauma).
NeglectFaltering growth, poor hygiene, missed appointments/immunisations, untreated dental caries, developmental delay.
SexualSTI, pregnancy in a young child, genital injury, sexualised behaviour.
Emotional/behaviouralWithdrawn, frozen watchfulness, self-harm, wetting.
Actions
  • Listen
  • Don't promise confidentiality
  • Document verbatim (dated, signed, body maps)
  • Ensure immediate safety (admit if needed)
  • Discuss with senior/named doctor for safeguarding
  • Refer to children's social services (± police).
  • Strategy meeting → Section 47 enquiry → child protection conference.
Doctor's role
  • Everyone's responsibility
  • Child's welfare is paramount (Children Act 1989/2004; Wales: Social Services and Well-being (Wales) Act 2014, Wales Safeguarding Procedures).
  • GMC: share information when needed to protect a child
  • Consent not required if seeking it would increase risk.

los.text: Explain normal and common abnormal findings in newborn infants and potential treatments options for common findings
los.html:
• Newborn and infant physical examination (NIPE) within 72 h, repeated at 6–8 weeks.
  • Normal variants: milia
    • Mongolian blue spots (document!)
    • erythema toxicum (day 2–3, resolves)
    • stork marks
    • physiological jaundice (after 24 h, resolves by 2 weeks)
    • breast engorgement/vaginal withdrawal bleed
    • caput succedaneum (crosses suture lines)
    • positional talipes (corrects passively)
    • umbilical hernia.
FindingSignificance / management
Jaundice <24 hAlways pathological (haemolysis: ABO/Rh, G6PD, sepsis). Serum bilirubin, phototherapy/exchange
Prolonged jaundice >14 d (>21 d preterm)Check conjugated bilirubin → biliary atresia (pale stools, dark urine) needs surgery (Kasai)
Absent red reflexCongenital cataract or retinoblastoma → urgent ophthalmology
Hip instability (Barlow/Ortolani)DDH → hip USS; Pavlik harness
Heart murmur/absent femoral pulsesCongenital heart disease, coarctation → echo. Pulse oximetry screening
Undescended testesReview at 6–8 weeks; refer if not descended by 3 months; orchidopexy 6–12 months
CephalhaematomaSubperiosteal bleed, doesn't cross sutures; jaundice risk
Cleft lip/palate, hypospadias (don't circumcise), structural talipes (Ponseti)Specialist referral
  • Other screening: hearing (OAE), heel prick (day 5) for CF, PKU, hypothyroidism, sickle cell, MCADD and others.

los.text: Describe modern concepts of childhood and the main tenets of the UN Convention of the Rights of the Child
los.html:
Modern concept(sociology of childhood)
  • Childhood is a social construction that varies by culture and history (Ariès).
  • Children are seen as active agents with their own rights and voices, not "adults in waiting" or property of parents.
UN Convention on the Rights of the Child (1989)
  • Ratified by the UK in 1991
  • Wales embedded it in law (Rights of Children and Young Persons (Wales) Measure 2011).
  • Covers everyone under 18.
  • 54 articles.
Four general principles
  • Non-discrimination (Art. 2).
  • Best interests of the child as a primary consideration (Art. 3).
  • Right to life, survival and development (Art. 6).
  • Right to be heard: views given due weight according to age and maturity (Art. 12).
Other key rights: health and healthcare (Art. 24), protection from abuse and neglect (Art. 19), education, play, family life, privacy.
Clinical relevanceInvolve children in decisions; Gillick competence and Fraser guidelines; safeguarding.

los.text: Describe the key stages of embryonic development (gastrulation, neurulation) and the formation of the embryonic and extra-embryonic membranes
los.html:
Week 1Fertilisation (ampulla) → cleavage → morula → blastocyst (inner cell mass = embryoblast; outer trophoblast) → implantation (~day 6–7).
Week 2 ("week of twos")Embryoblast → bilaminar disc (epiblast + hypoblast); trophoblast → cytotrophoblast + syncytiotrophoblast (secretes hCG); two cavities (amniotic cavity, yolk sac).
Week 3 – gastrulation
  • Primitive streak forms on epiblast; cells migrate to form the trilaminar disc:
  • Ectoderm: epidermis, nervous system, neural crest.
  • Mesoderm: notochord, somites (muscle, bone, dermis), intermediate (kidneys, gonads), lateral plate (body wall, heart, blood vessels, serosa).
  • Endoderm: gut epithelium, liver, pancreas, lungs, thyroid.
Neurulation(weeks 3–4)
  • Notochord induces overlying ectoderm → neural plate → neural folds → neural tube (closes cranially ~day 25, caudally ~day 27).
  • Failure → anencephaly / spina bifida (prevent with folic acid 400 μg, 5 mg if high risk).
  • Neural crest → PNS ganglia, melanocytes, adrenal medulla, facial bones, cardiac outflow septum.
Extra-embryonic membranes
  • Amnion (fluid-filled sac)
  • Chorion (fetal part of placenta; chorionic villi)
  • Yolk sac (early blood cells, primordial germ cells)
  • Allantois (→ urachus; umbilical vessels).
Weeks 3–8Embryonic period (organogenesis): most vulnerable to teratogens.

los.text: Explain how the principles of genetic transmission relate to specific genetic defects, their mode of transmission and clinical effects
los.html:
InheritancePatternExamples
Autosomal dominantEvery generation; 50% risk to offspring; M = F; variable penetrance/expressivityHuntington's, ADPKD, Marfan, NF1, familial hypercholesterolaemia, BRCA1/2
Autosomal recessiveSkips generations; carriers unaffected; 25% risk if both carriers; consanguinityCystic fibrosis, sickle cell, β-thalassaemia, PKU, haemochromatosis
X-linked recessiveMostly males; no male-to-male transmission; carrier mothers → 50% of sons affectedDuchenne, haemophilia A/B, G6PD deficiency, red–green colour blindness
X-linked dominantAffected father → all daughtersHypophosphataemic rickets, Rett (lethal in males)
MitochondrialMaternal transmission only; heteroplasmyMELAS, Leber's hereditary optic neuropathy
Chromosomal
  • Aneuploidy from non-disjunction (↑ maternal age): Down (trisomy 21), Edwards (18), Patau (13), Turner (45,X), Klinefelter (47,XXY)
  • Robertsonian translocation (familial Down's)
  • Deletions (22q11 DiGeorge).
MutationsPoint (missense, nonsense, silent), frameshift, trinucleotide repeat expansion with anticipation (Huntington's, fragile X, myotonic dystrophy).
Epigenetics/imprintingGene expression depends on parent of origin. 15q11–13 deletion: paternal → Prader–Willi, maternal → Angelman. Also uniparental disomy.
MultifactorialPolygenic + environment (neural tube defects, cleft lip, T2DM).

los.text: Explain the mechanisms by which mutations and other genetic changes can lead to cancer
los.html:
• Cancer = accumulation of somatic (± inherited) mutations that give cells the "hallmarks": sustained proliferation
  • Evading growth suppressors
  • Resisting death
  • Replicative immortality (telomerase)
  • Angiogenesis
  • Invasion/metastasis
  • Plus genome instability
  • Inflammation
  • Immune evasion
  • Altered metabolism.
Oncogenes(gain of function, dominant: one hit enough)RAS (pancreas, colon), MYC (Burkitt t(8;14)), HER2/ERBB2 amplification (breast), BCR-ABL t(9;22) (CML), BRAF (melanoma), EGFR (lung).
Tumour suppressor genes(loss of function, recessive at cell level)
  • Knudson's two-hit hypothesis.
  • Inherited first hit → early, multiple, bilateral tumours.
  • Examples: TP53 (Li–Fraumeni), RB1 (retinoblastoma), APC (FAP), BRCA1/2 (breast/ovarian; homologous recombination repair), VHL.
DNA repair genesMismatch repair (MLH1, MSH2 → Lynch syndrome, microsatellite instability).
Other mechanismsChromosomal translocations, gene amplification, epigenetic silencing (promoter hypermethylation), viral oncogenes (HPV E6/E7 inactivate p53/Rb; EBV; HBV).
Multistep progressione.g. colorectal adenoma–carcinoma sequence (APC → KRAS → TP53).
ClinicalGenetic testing and screening of families, targeted therapies (trastuzumab, imatinib), PARP inhibitors in BRCA.
